Sunday, October 25, 2026 Daily Digest

Elvis Estate Sues Anthropic for $41M Over AI Training, US and China Form Competing AI Blocs, Agentic AI Used in Live Cyberattacks

Today's top stories in AI + enterprise tech

1

Elvis Presley Estate Sues Anthropic for $41M, Alleging Claude Was Trained on 274 Songs Without Permission

Authentic Brands Group, which controls the Elvis Presley catalog, filed ABE EPE LLC v. Anthropic on October 23, alleging that Claude was trained on 274 Presley songs — from "Can't Help Falling in Love" to "A Little Less Conversation" — without permission. The suit seeks $150,000 per song, totaling roughly $41 million, and claims Claude can still produce rewritten versions that preserve recognizable song structures. Attorney Richard Busch leads the case, marking the eighth AI music copyright suit filed by Adams & Reese this year. The lawsuit represents the entertainment industry's escalating legal offensive against foundation model companies, testing whether training on copyrighted works constitutes fair use. For enterprise AI teams, the case has implications beyond music: if courts rule that model training requires licensing, the cost structure of deploying AI — and the liability exposure for using models trained on unlicensed data — could shift dramatically. The timing, weeks before Anthropic's targeted mid-November IPO, adds strategic pressure.

2

US and China Form Competing AI Blocs, Forcing Allies to Choose Between Pax Silica and WAICO

An AP investigation details how the US-led Pax Silica group and China's World AI Cooperation Organization (WAICO) — with 28 founding members including Pakistan and Russia — are forcing countries to pick sides in the emerging AI cold war. The State Department warned that nations "cannot be trusted partners in Pax Silica while substantively engaging in initiatives that advance a competing vision for super intelligence." Kazakhstan joined both blocs within three weeks, visiting Washington in June then signing WAICO in Shanghai, illustrating the impossible position many countries face. The bifurcation has direct enterprise implications: organizations operating across geopolitical boundaries may need to maintain separate AI stacks for different markets, data sovereignty requirements could fragment further, and vendor relationships may become geopolitically constrained. The bloc formation also signals that AI governance won't emerge from global consensus — it will fragment along the same lines as the broader tech decoupling between the US and China.

3

Palo Alto Unit 42: Agentic AI Used in Live PHP Exploit Attacks, Reaching Active Directory in Two Hours

Palo Alto Networks Unit 42 published an updated threat brief documenting attackers using an agentic AI platform in post-exploitation of CVE-2026-109618/109619 — the "Black October" PHP vulnerabilities disclosed earlier this week. In one case involving a European government entity, the attackers achieved NTLM relay into Active Directory within two hours of initial compromise. The behavioral signature is distinctive: command batches wrapped in machine-readable formats suggesting automated decision-making rather than human operators. This marks one of the first documented cases of AI agents being used autonomously in live cyberattacks — not just for reconnaissance or phishing generation, but for actual exploit chain execution. The speed and efficiency of the attack raises urgent questions for enterprise security teams: if AI can compress the timeline from initial access to domain compromise, traditional detection and response windows may be insufficient. Security teams should assume attackers are already using AI assistance and adjust monitoring for the velocity these tools enable.

4

63% of US Voters Oppose AI Data Centers Within 10 Miles — Bipartisan Backlash Against Infrastructure Build

A CNBC All-America Economic Survey found 63% of registered voters oppose an AI data center within 10 miles of their home, while only 13% support one — pointing to voter backlash against the AI infrastructure buildout heading into the midterms. The opposition is bipartisan: 80% of Democrats oppose, and even among MAGA supporters only 29% would back a nearby facility while 40% oppose. Hart Research and Public Opinion Strategies polled 1,000 registered voters October 14-18. The findings create a political constraint on the AI infrastructure race: communities are increasingly organized against data center development, citing power consumption, water usage, and quality-of-life concerns. For enterprise AI leaders, the data center opposition means capacity constraints may persist longer than projected as permitting faces local resistance. The political dimension adds uncertainty to infrastructure planning — cloud providers and enterprises may find that "sold out through 2027" extends further as new builds face community opposition.

5

Cloudflare CEO Warns AI-Discovered Vulnerabilities Will Make "Every Week Feel Like the Sky Is Falling"

A Reuters feature interviews seven cybersecurity professionals who expect AI-discovered software flaws to keep triggering global outages after this week's PHP, Node.js, Plex, LiteLLM, and Railway disclosures. Cloudflare CEO Matthew Prince said he's aware of "a bunch of additional severe vulnerabilities" and predicted "a couple years where every single week it's going to feel like the sky is falling." VulnCheck research due in coming days will show AI-found flaws roughly doubled year-on-year. The warning underscores a fundamental asymmetry: AI tools for finding vulnerabilities are advancing faster than the ability to patch them. For enterprise security teams, this means continuous discovery of zero-days across the software supply chain, compressed patching windows, and increased exposure for organizations running vulnerable dependencies. The shift requires moving from periodic security reviews to continuous vulnerability management — and accepting that some level of exposure is now the permanent operating condition.

💡 My Take

The AI security reckoning is accelerating faster than most enterprises are prepared for. The Unit 42 report documenting agentic AI in live cyberattacks isn't a theoretical warning — it's here, now, with attackers reaching Active Directory in two hours. Combined with Cloudflare's prediction of weekly "sky is falling" vulnerability disclosures, the security posture required for AI-era operations is fundamentally different from what most organizations have in place. The Elvis lawsuit against Anthropic, meanwhile, represents a different kind of reckoning — the legal one. If courts rule that training requires licensing, the entire foundation model economics shift, and enterprises using these models inherit liability exposure they may not have priced in. The geopolitical story is equally consequential: the US-China AI bloc formation means enterprises operating globally will face increasing pressure to pick sides, maintain separate stacks, or accept operational constraints in certain markets. The 63% opposition to data centers adds an unexpected constraint to all of this — the infrastructure needed to run AI at scale faces political headwinds that could extend capacity shortages beyond current projections. We're entering a period where the second-order effects of AI — legal, security, geopolitical, infrastructural — matter as much as the technology itself.
